books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Articles VIII, IX, XI, February 2, 1848
An Act for the Government and Protection of Indians, California, April 22, 1850
Louise Amelia Knapp Smith Clappe, letter, November 25, 1851
E. Gilman, map of the United States after the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, 1848

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources (see each document's sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Mexican-American War changed the lives of the people living in the territory the United States acquired from Mexico in the period 1846–1855.

documents.title: The Capitulation of Cahuenga
documents.source: Articles of Capitulation at the Rancho of Cahuenga, January 13, 1847, between commissioners of Lt. Col. John C. Frémont and Gen. Andrés Pico. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The surrender terms ending the fighting in California, agreed by Frémont's officers and the Californio commander Pico.
documents.text: Article 1. The Commissioners on the part of the Californians agree that their entire force shall, on presentation of themselves to Lieutenant-Colonel Fremont, deliver up their artillery and public arms, and they shall return peaceably to their homes, conforming to the laws and regulations of the United States, and not again take up arms during the war between the United States and Mexico. . . . Art. 2. The Commissioners on the part of Lieutenant-Colonel Fremont agree and bind themselves on the fulfillment of the first article by the Californians, that they shall be guaranteed protection of life and property whether on parole or otherwise. . . . Art. 5. That, in virtue of the aforesaid articles, equal rights and privilege are vouchsafed to every citizen of California, as are enjoyed by the citizens of the United States of North America.

documents.title: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Article VIII
documents.source: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, February 2, 1848, Article VIII (ratified text). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The peace treaty ending the war, setting out what would happen to Mexicans living in the ceded lands.
documents.text: Mexicans now established in territories previously belonging to Mexico, and which remain for the future within the limits of the United States, as defined by the present treaty, shall be free to continue where they now reside, or to remove at any time to the Mexican Republic, retaining the property which they possess in the said territories. . . . Those who shall prefer to remain in the said territories may either retain the title and rights of Mexican citizens, or acquire those of citizens of the United States. But they shall be under the obligation to make their election within one year from the date of the exchange of ratifications of this treaty.

documents.title: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Article IX
documents.source: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, February 2, 1848, Article IX (ratified text). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The same treaty's promise about the future of the Mexicans who stayed in the ceded lands.
documents.text: The Mexicans who, in the territories aforesaid, shall not preserve the character of citizens of the Mexican Republic, conformably with what is stipulated in the preceding article, shall be incorporated into the Union of the United States, and be admitted at the proper time (to be judged of by the Congress of the United States) to the enjoyment of all the rights of citizens of the United States, according to the principles of the Constitution; and in the mean time, shall be maintained and protected in the free enjoyment of their liberty and property, and secured in the free exercise of their religion without restriction.

documents.title: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Article XI
documents.source: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, February 2, 1848, Article XI (ratified text). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The same treaty's promise about Indian peoples living in the new American territory, and raids across the new border into Mexico.
documents.text: Considering that a great part of the territories, which, by the present treaty, are to be comprehended for the future within the limits of the United States, is now occupied by savage tribes, who will hereafter be under the exclusive control of the Government of the United States, and whose incursions within the territory of Mexico would be prejudicial in the extreme, it is solemnly agreed that all such incursions shall be forcibly restrained by the Government of the United States whensoever this may be necessary.

documents.title: California's Act for the Government and Protection of Indians
documents.source: An Act for the Government and Protection of Indians, Chapter 133, Statutes of California, April 22, 1850, Section 3. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: One of the first laws of the new state of California, passed by a legislature dominated by white newcomers from the United States.
documents.text: Any person having or hereafter obtaining a minor Indian, male or female, from the parents or relations of such Indian minor, and wishing to keep it, such person shall go before a Justice of the Peace in his Township, with the parents or friends of the child, and if the Justice of the Peace becomes satisfied that no compulsory means have been used to obtain the child from its parents or friends, shall enter on record, in a book kept for that purpose, the sex and probable age of the child, and shall give to such person a certificate, authorizing him or her to have the care, custody, control, and earnings of such minor, until he or she obtain the age of majority.

documents.title: Dame Shirley tries the mines
documents.source: Louise Amelia Knapp Smith Clappe (“Dame Shirley”), letter from Indian Bar, California, November 25, 1851, published in The Pioneer, 1854. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A letter from a newcomer's wife at the diggings, written to her sister in the East under the pen name Dame Shirley.
documents.text: Nothing of importance has happened since I last wrote you, except that I have become a mineress, that is, if the having washed a pan of dirt with my own hands, and procured therefrom three dollars and twenty-five cents in gold-dust, which I shall inclose in this letter, will entitle me to the name. I can truly say, with the blacksmith's apprentice at the close of his first day's work at the anvil, that I am sorry I learned the trade; for I wet my feet, tore my dress, spoilt a pair of new gloves, nearly froze my fingers, got an awful headache, took cold, and lost a valuable breastpin, in this my labor of love.

documents.title: Gilman's map of the United States after the treaty
documents.source: E. Gilman, map of the United States after the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, published 1848. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A commercial map published the year of the treaty, showing the new United States with California and New Mexico Territory inside its borders.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the development in question occurred, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the annexation of Texas, Manifest Destiny, or the sectional balance before the war.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about the prompt.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Compromise of 1850, the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, or the Dred Scott decision of 1857.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The war changed life in the acquired lands profoundly but unevenly — newcomers found opportunity, Californios found their promised rights fading, and California Indians found a new government that legalized their exploitation.
Context: Before the war the lands were Mexico's northern provinces, home to Californios, Pueblo and other Native peoples, and a small number of American settlers; the war transferred them to the United States in 1848.
Evidence: Documents 1-3 show the promises — Cahuenga's equal rights, the treaty's protection of property and choice of citizenship, and the promise of full citizenship and religious freedom. Documents 4-6 show the reality — the pledge to stop raids that the United States could not keep, California's 1850 law binding Indian children to white holders, and a newcomer's letter from a mining camp that had not existed three years earlier. Document 7 shows the new map itself.
Beyond the documents: The Gadsden Purchase of 1853 released the United States from its Article XI promise, and California's Indian population fell from about 150,000 in 1848 to under 30,000 by the Civil War.
Sourcing: Cahuenga and the treaty were bargains struck by soldiers and diplomats; the 1850 act was written by the newcomers' own legislature; Dame Shirley wrote home to family, not for publication.
Complexity: The same transfer that opened the mines to newcomers closed the old order for the people already there — the promises were real on paper and thin in practice, and the difference fell hardest on those with the least power.
